# Understanding Hallucinations for Federal Employees

<!-- vimeo: 1216129104 | track: English (auto-generated) -->

[▶ Watch on Vimeo](https://vimeo.com/1216129104)

<details>
<summary>자막: Understanding Hallucinations for Federal Employees</summary>

AI can produce an answer that sounds polished, specific, and confident, and still be wrong. That kind of false, fabricated, or unsupported output is often called a hallucination. Why does it happen? Language models generate responses from patterns. Fluency is not the same as evidence. A useful answer can include an incorrect date, a made-up quotation, a nonexistent citation, or an overconfident conclusion. Consider a fictional analyst at the Federal Civic Services office. She asks an AI tool to summarize a travel reimbursement policy. The response looks authoritative and cites Directive 22-17, effective October 1st. But that directive does not exist. If copied into a briefing, one invented detail could become an official-looking error. Watch closely when an answer includes precise dates, names, numbers, quotations, or citations without links to supporting material. Other warning signs include vague sourcing, claims that change when you ask again, or certainty about an ambiguous question. Confidence is a writing style, not proof. Use a simple verification routine. First, pause before relying on the answer. Second, compare every consequential claim with an authoritative source. Third, ask the tool to identify uncertainty and provide supporting citations, but open those sources and check them yourself. Fourth, separate verified facts from analysis or inference. And when the stakes involve benefits, procurement, personnel, law, safety, policy, or public communication, route the work through the required human review. Use only information approved for your environment, and follow your agency's data handling rules. AI can accelerate research and drafting, but it does not replace accountability. Before you rely, brief, send, or act, verify the claim, verify the source, and apply human judgment.
